questions.stem: A 32-year-old male presents with weakness and numbness in his right arm following a motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm and weakness of elbow flexion. Which part of the brachial plexus does not give branches?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Division

 

The brachial plexus is organized into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches. Divisions of the brachial plexus do not give off any branches. The divisions are formed from the splitting of the trunks into anterior and posterior divisions, which then unite to form the cords. It is at the level of the cords and roots where branches arise that innervate various parts of the upper limb, but the divisions serve primarily as passageways without branching out into nerves.  It is the only part of the brachial plexus that does not give off branches.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Roots: The roots of the brachial plexus do give off branches, including the dorsal scapular nerve and the long thoracic nerve, which innervate muscles such as the rhomboids and serratus anterior.
 

Option B. Trunks: The upper trunk of the brachial plexus gives off the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius. These branches innervate important muscles in the shoulder region.
 

Option D. Cords: The cords of the brachial plexus give off several important branches, including the lateral pectoral nerve, the medial pectoral nerve, and the thoracodorsal nerve, which are crucial for upper limb innervation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The divisions of the brachial plexus do not give rise to any branches, unlike the roots, trunks, and cords, which all contribute branches to various nerves of the upper limb.

questions.stem: Pronator quadratus receives innervation from a nerve which also supplies? A. Flexor digitorum superficialisB. Flexor pollicis longusC. Flexor carpi ulnarisD. Flexor digitorum profundus in the middle fingerE. Palmaris longus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) B, D

 

The pronator quadratus is innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve, which is a branch of the median nerve. This same nerve also supplies the flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of the flexor digitorum profundus, specifically the part that flexes the index and middle fingers The anterior interosseous nerve provides motor innervation to these muscles, which are important for fine motor control of the fingers and thumb.

 

Other Options:

 

A. Flexor digitorum superficialis: While this muscle is innervated by the median nerve, it is not supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve but rather by the main trunk of the median nerve.
 

C. Flexor carpi ulnaris: This muscle is innervated by the ulnar nerve, not the median or anterior interosseous nerve.
 

E. Palmaris longus: This muscle is also supplied by the median nerve, but not by the anterior interosseous nerve; it is innervated by the main trunk of the median nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The pronator quadratus is innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve, which also supplies the flexor pollicis longus and the lateral part of the flexor digitorum profundus (middle and index fingers).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain and dyspnea. He has a history of hypertension and is a current smoker. On physical examination, he appears anxious and diaphoretic. Vital signs are significant for tachycardia and tachypnea. Auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds on the left side. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Further evaluation reveals a left-sided superior intercostal vein anomaly. Which vessel does the left superior intercostal vein normally drain into?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Brachiocephalic vein

 

The left superior intercostal vein is responsible for draining blood from the upper intercostal spaces (typically the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th intercostal spaces) on the left side of the thoracic wall. This vein passes over the aortic arch and empties into the left brachiocephalic vein. The left brachiocephalic vein is a major venous structure that carries deoxygenated blood from the left side of the thorax and upper body to the superior vena cava, which then returns the blood to the heart.

 

The left superior intercostal vein does not drain into the azygous or hemi azygous system, which typically manages venous drainage from the right and lower left thoracic regions, respectively. Instead, it directly connects with the left brachiocephalic vein,

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Azygous vein: The azygous vein drains the right-sided intercostal veins and forms a part of the azygous venous system on the right side of the body. It does not drain the left superior intercostal vein.
 

Option B. Hemi azygous vein: The hemi azygous vein drains the lower left posterior intercostal veins and does not connect with the left superior intercostal vein. The hemi azygous vein joins the azygous system lower in the thoracic cavity.
 

Option C. Internal thoracic vein: The internal thoracic vein drains the anterior chest wall and intercostal spaces, not the posterior intercostal veins like the left superior intercostal vein.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The left superior intercostal vein typically drains into the left brachiocephalic vein, forming a direct connection between the upper left intercostal spaces and the central venous system.

questions.stem: A patient with syphilis is unable to walk with closed eyes and presents with a stomping gait. Name the tract involved in the given condition:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Dorsal column tract

 

The dorsal column tract is responsible for transmitting sensory information related to fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (the sense of body position). In patients with syphilis, especially those with tabes dorsalis (a late-stage neurosyphilis complication), there is damage to the dorsal column tract, leading to the loss of proprioception. This results in a stomping gait because the patient compensates for the lack of position sense by forcefully placing their feet on the ground. The inability to walk with closed eyes is due to the loss of proprioception, as patients heavily rely on visual input to maintain balance when this sensory pathway is impaired.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Spinocerebellar tract: This tract is involved in unconscious proprioception and coordination of movement, but damage here typically causes ataxia rather than the specific sensory loss seen in tabes dorsalis.
 

Option C. Lateral spinothalamic tract: This tract transmits pain and temperature sensations, and its damage results in the loss of these sensations, not proprioception or vibration sense.
 

Option D. Vestibulospinal tract: This tract is involved in maintaining balance and posture by influencing motor neurons, but it does not transmit proprioceptive or vibration information. Dysfunction in this tract leads to balance problems but not sensory deficits like the loss of proprioception.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Damage to the dorsal column tract, particularly seen in conditions like tabes dorsalis (a complication of syphilis), results in the loss of proprioception, causing difficulty walking with closed eyes and a characteristic stomping gait.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of altered taste sensation on the left side of her tongue. She reports recent dental surgery on that side. On examination, taste sensation is intact on the tongue bilaterally. Which cranial nerve is not associated with the taste pathway?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) XII

 

The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) is responsible for motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue and is not involved in taste sensation. 

 

Other Options

 

The nerves involved in the taste pathway include:

 

Option A. Cranial nerve V (Trigeminal nerve): While not directly involved in taste, the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve carries sensory information (touch, pain, temperature) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

 

Option B. Cranial nerve IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve): Responsible for taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.

 

Option C. Cranial nerve X (Vagus nerve): Contributes to taste sensation from the base of the tongue and the epiglottis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) is not involved in the taste pathway; its function is purely motor, controlling tongue movement.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female presents to the orthopedic clinic with persistent wrist pain following a fall on an outstretched hand. On examination, there is tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox and limited range of motion of the wrist joint. Radiographs reveal a fracture of the scaphoid bone. Which bone is not typically involved in the formation of the wrist joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ulna

 

The ulna is not typically involved in the direct formation of the wrist joint. The wrist joint, also known as the radiocarpal joint, is primarily formed by the distal end of the radius and the proximal row of carpal bones, including the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetral bones. A fibrocartilaginous structure known as the articular disc (or triangular fibrocartilage) separates the distal end of the ulna from the carpal bones,

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Scaphoid: The scaphoid is one of the carpal bones that directly articulates with the radius to form part of the wrist joint.
 

Option C. Radius: The radius is a major bone involved in forming the radiocarpal joint, as it directly articulates with the carpal bones.
 

Option D. Triquetral: The triquetral is a carpal bone involved in the wrist joint, as it articulates with the articular disc and the lunate to form part of the joint.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ulna is not typically involved in the formation of the wrist joint due to the presence of the articular disc, which separates it from the carpal bones.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents to the primary care clinic with lower back pain radiating down his left leg. He reports a history of heavy lifting at work. On physical examination, there is tenderness over the lumbar vertebrae with limited lumbar spine flexion due to pain. Which anatomical curvature is normally observed in the lumbar spine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lordosis

 

 

The normal curvature of the lumbar spine is lordosis, which refers to the inward (concave) curvature of the spine in the lumbar region. This curvature helps to maintain balance and absorb shock during activities such as walking and lifting. In the image provided, we can clearly observe the lumbar region exhibiting lordosis with an angle of about 45°. This is a physiological curvature essential for proper posture and spinal function.

 

In cases of lower back pain, especially related to heavy lifting, the lumbar lordosis can be strained, leading to discomfort and pain, as seen in the patient's symptoms.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option B. Scoliosis refers to an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.

 

Option C. Kyphosis is the outward curvature typically found in the thoracic spine (a posterior convex curve).

 

Option D. Recurvatum refers to hyperextension, typically associated with joints, particularly the knee, and is not related to the curvature of the spine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The normal curvature of the lumbar spine is lordosis, which helps with weight distribution and maintaining proper posture.

questions.stem: All the given muscles help in inversion of the foot except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Peroneus longus

 

The peroneus longus (also known as the fibularis longus) is a muscle involved in eversion of the foot, not inversion. It plays a significant role in stabilizing the lateral aspect of the foot and helps with plantarflexion as well. Therefore, it does not contribute to foot inversion.

 

Other Options:

 

The muscles that assist in inversion of the foot include:

 

Option A. Tibialis anterior: This muscle primarily dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot.

 

Option B. Tibialis posterior: A powerful invertor of the foot and also supports the arch.

 

Option C. Extensor halluces longus: Though mainly involved in dorsiflexion of the big toe, it also contributes to slight inversion of the foot.

 

Thus, the peroneus longus is the only muscle listed that is involved in eversion, not inversion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The peroneus longus is involved in eversion of the foot, while muscles like the tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior contribute to inversion.

questions.stem: Arrange the given stages of spermatogenesis in the correct sequence: A. SpermatidB. SpermatozoaC. SpermatogoniumD. Spermatocyte
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C → D → A → B

 

Spermatogenesis is the process by which sperm cells are produced and developed in the testes. The correct sequence of stages in spermatogenesis is as follows:

 

C. Spermatogonium: These are the diploid stem cells located in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. They divide by mitosis to give rise to primary spermatocytes.

 

D. Spermatocyte: The spermatogonium differentiates into spermatocytes (primary and secondary), which undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells known as spermatids.

 

A. Spermatid: After meiosis, the resulting spermatids are round haploid cells that undergo further maturation.

 

B. Spermatozoa: The spermatids mature into spermatozoa (mature sperm cells), which are then capable of fertilizing an egg.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of spermatogenesis is Spermatogonium → Spermatocyte → Spermatid → Spermatozoa.

questions.stem: After parotidectomy, a patient complains of loss of sensation while shaving. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Great auricular nerve

 

The great auricular nerve is commonly affected during a parotidectomy, as it runs along the surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid region, the angle of the mandible, and the ear. Injury to this nerve during surgery can result in loss of sensation over the shaving area (angle of the mandible and lower ear), which aligns with the patient’s complaint of loss of sensation while shaving. The great auricular nerve is derived from the cervical plexus (C2 and C3) and is vulnerable in procedures involving the parotid gland.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Auriculotemporal nerve: This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin over the temple and is associated with Frey's syndrome but is not typically involved in sensation loss at the angle of the mandible.
 

Option C. Facial nerve: The facial nerve is responsible for motor control of facial muscles, not sensory input. Damage to this nerve would result in facial weakness, not sensory loss.
 

Option D. Mandibular nerve: While the mandibular nerve provides sensory and motor innervation to the jaw and lower face, the great auricular nerve is more directly related to sensation at the angle of the mandible.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The great auricular nerve is commonly injured during parotid surgery, leading to loss of sensation in the shaving area (angle of the mandible and ear).

questions.stemHtml: Which structure passes through the marked opening?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thoracic duct

 

The structure shown in the image is the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct passes through this opening along with the aorta and the azygous vein. The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body and drains lymph into the venous system at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

 

This opening is at the T12 vertebral level, and it is distinct from other diaphragmatic openings, such as the caval opening at T8 (for the inferior vena cava) and the esophageal hiatus at T10 (for the esophagus and vagus nerves).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vena cava: The vena cava passes through the caval opening at the T8 level, not the aortic hiatus.
 

Option C. Esophagus: The esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus at the T10 level.
 

Option D. Phrenic nerve: The right phrenic nerve passes through the caval opening along with the inferior vena cava, while the left phrenic nerve does not pass through this particular opening.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the T12 level, along with the aorta and azygous vein.

questions.stem: A patient underwent a left submandibular gland excision during which the hypoglossal nerve was injured. Which of the following deficits would be seen in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side

options.label: B
options.text: Deviated tongue to the same side

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue

questions.answerText: Deviated tongue to the same side
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Deviated tongue to the same side

 

The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) provides motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue. If the hypoglossal nerve is injured during a left submandibular gland excision, the affected side of the tongue will experience muscle weakness or paralysis. When the patient attempts to protrude their tongue, it will deviate to the same side as the injury (in this case, the left side) due to the unopposed action of the muscles on the opposite side.

 

The muscles on the non-affected side will push the tongue toward the paralyzed side.

 

This is a hallmark sign of hypoglossal nerve damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Deviated tongue to the contralateral side: The tongue deviates toward the same side as the injury, not the contralateral side.
 

Option C. Inability to protrude tongue: Although tongue movement is weakened on the injured side, complete inability to protrude the tongue is not typically seen.
 

Option D. Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue: Taste sensation in the posterior one-third of the tongue is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), not the hypoglossal nerve, so this would not be affected in hypoglossal nerve injury.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Injury to the hypoglossal nerve results in tongue deviation toward the same side as the injury due to paralysis of the tongue muscles on the affected side.

questions.stemHtml: A patient developed the following deformity after overhead weightlifting & pushing exercises. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Serratus anterior

 

The image shows a winged scapula, a condition commonly caused by injury or weakness of the serratus anterior muscle. This muscle is responsible for holding the scapula against the thoracic wall. It is innervated by the long thoracic nerve, which is vulnerable during overhead lifting or pushing exercises.

 

When the serratus anterior is weak or paralyzed, the medial border of the scapula protrudes outward, causing the characteristic winging seen in this patient. This condition typically arises when the long thoracic nerve is injured, such as during excessive or improper overhead weight-lifting activities.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Latissimus dorsi: This muscle is involved in shoulder adduction, extension, and internal rotation, but it does not stabilize the scapula against the ribcage.
 

Option B. Trapezius: Although the trapezius plays a role in scapular movement, damage to this muscle does not result in a winged scapula.
 

Option D. Supraspinatus: This muscle is part of the rotator cuff and helps with shoulder abduction but is not involved in scapular stabilization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Weakness or injury to the serratus anterior muscle, typically due to damage to the long thoracic nerve, leads to a winged scapula.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to a murmur noted by the parents. On auscultation, a continuous machinery-like murmur is heard over the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography reveals a patent ductus arteriosus. Which pharyngeal arch artery does the ductus arteriosus develop from?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 6

 

The ductus arteriosus develops from the 6th pharyngeal arch artery. This fetal blood vessel connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, allowing blood to bypass the lungs, which are not used during fetal life. After birth, it normally closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. In cases where the ductus arteriosus remains patent (PDA), it results in a continuous "machinery-like" murmur, as heard in this infant. This is a key anatomical structure involved in fetal circulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3: The 3rd pharyngeal arch artery forms the common carotid artery and part of the internal carotid artery, not the ductus arteriosus.

 

Option B. 4: The 4th pharyngeal arch artery contributes to the formation of the aortic arch and the right subclavian artery.

 

Option C. 5: The 5th pharyngeal arch artery usually regresses and does not form any significant structures in humans.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ductus arteriosus develops from the 6th pharyngeal arch artery, and its failure to close after birth results in a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), characterized by a continuous machinery-like murmur.

questions.stemHtml: The tissue in the image is found in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Epiphyseal plates

 

The tissue in the image is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, which is present in epiphyseal plates (growth plates). Hyaline cartilage is known for its glassy, smooth appearance and its role in bone growth during childhood and adolescence. The chondrocytes, seen within lacunae, are embedded in a matrix that provides support and flexibility to the developing bone.

 

 

Epiphyseal plates are responsible for longitudinal bone growth. They are present between the diaphysis and epiphysis of long bones and are essential for bone elongation during development.

 

The matrix of hyaline cartilage stains pink with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain, which is consistent with the features of epiphyseal plate cartilage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Articular disc: The articular disc contains fibrocartilage, which has a more fibrous appearance and is found in joints like the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).

 

Option B. Intervertebral disc: The intervertebral disc consists of fibrocartilage in the annulus fibrosus, which does not resemble the hyaline cartilage

 

Option D. Pinna of ear: The pinna contains elastic cartilage, which has a different structure characterized by the presence of elastic fibers 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The tissue in the image is hyaline cartilage, which is typically found in epiphyseal plates, where it plays a crucial role in bone growth.

questions.stem: In humans, many diseases are associated with failure of migration of neural crest cells. Neural crest cell migration is due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Hyaluronic acid


Hyaluronic acid is a critical component of the extracellular matrix that provides the physical and chemical signals required for neural crest cells to migrate during embryonic development. It acts as a scaffold, allowing cells to move through tissues. Disruption in hyaluronic acid synthesis or function can result in congenital anomalies due to impaired neural crest migration, as these cells contribute to the formation of various structures, including craniofacial components and parts of the heart.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Heparin: Heparin is an anticoagulant that is not directly involved in cell migration processes such as neural crest migration.

 

Option B. Heparan sulfate: Heparan sulfate is involved in cell signaling and development but is not the main mediator for the migration of neural crest cells. It primarily plays a role in growth factor binding and angiogenesis.

 

Option D. Dermatan sulfate: Dermatan sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan involved in the structure of connective tissue but does not play a primary role in the migration of neural crest cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neural crest cells migrate during embryogenesis with the aid of hyaluronic acid, which provides an essential framework in the extracellular matrix. Defects in this migration can lead to a variety of congenital disorders affecting craniofacial, cardiac, and other tissues.

questions.stemHtml: Which muscle is attached to the given pointed structure of the femur bone?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Iliopsoas

 

The lesser trochanter of the femur is the site of attachment for the iliopsoas muscle. The iliopsoas muscle is composed of the psoas major and the iliacus muscles, which converge and attach to the lesser trochanter. This muscle is primarily responsible for hip flexion and plays a crucial role in walking and maintaining posture.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gluteus maximus: This muscle attaches to the gluteal tuberosity and the iliotibial band, not the lesser trochanter.

 

Option B. Adductor magnus: This muscle attaches to the linea aspera and the adductor tubercle of the femur, not the lesser trochanter.

 

Option C. Quadriceps femoris: This muscle group attaches to the patella via the quadriceps tendon and does not attach to the lesser trochanter.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The iliopsoas muscle attaches to the lesser trochanter of the femur, and its primary function is hip flexion.

questions.stemHtml: The type of epithelium as shown in the image below is present in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Urinary bladder

 

The image shows transitional epithelium, which is a specialized type of stratified epithelium that lines the urinary system, including the urinary bladder, ureters, and part of the urethra. This type of epithelium is unique in its ability to stretch and accommodate fluctuating volumes of urine. It appears dome-shaped when relaxed and flattened when stretched, allowing the bladder to expand and contract as needed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Duodenum: The duodenum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, not transitional epithelium.

 

Option B. Common bile duct: The bile duct is lined by simple columnar epithelium, not transitional epithelium.

 

Option C. Skin: The skin is composed of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, not transitional epithelium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Transitional epithelium is present in the urinary bladder, where it allows for expansion and contraction depending on the volume of urine.

questions.stem: A student, after a heavy lunch from the hostel, got ready for his afternoon class. He sat on the first bench and began to take notes. After a while, he yawned widely. To his surprise, he could not close his mouth. The jaw was stuck. Which of the following statement is not true in the above scenario?

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of anterior dislocation of temporomandibular joint

options.label: B
options.text: Temporomandibular joint is a bicondylar type of synovial joint

options.label: C
options.text: Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible

options.label: D
options.text: Sphenomandibular ligament is situated medial to temporomandibular joint

questions.answerText: Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Contraction of medial pterygoid depresses the mandible

 

In this scenario, the patient is experiencing an anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). This typically happens when the mandible is moved excessively forward, such as during a wide yawn. The lateral pterygoid muscle contracts and pulls the articular disc and the mandibular condyle forward, causing the jaw to lock in a protruded position. To close the mouth, the condyle must be repositioned back into the mandibular fossa.

 

The temporomandibular joint is indeed a bicondylar synovial joint that allows for both hinging (elevation and depression) and gliding (protraction and retraction) movements.

 

The sphenomandibular ligament is located medial to the TMJ, playing a role in stabilizing the joint.

 

The incorrect statement is that the medial pterygoid muscle depresses the mandible. In fact, the medial pterygoid is involved in elevation of the mandible, not depression. Depression of the mandible is primarily achieved by the lateral pterygoid muscle along with gravity and the action of suprahyoid muscles.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. This is a case of anterior dislocation of temporomandibular joint: This is correct, as the clinical scenario describes a typical anterior dislocation where the patient is unable to close their mouth.
 

Option B. Temporomandibular joint is a bicondylar type of synovial joint: This is true, as the TMJ allows both hinging and gliding movements.
 

Option D. Sphenomandibular ligament is situated medial to temporomandibular joint: This statement is true, as the sphenomandibular ligament lies medial to the TMJ.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial pterygoid muscle elevates the mandible, while depression is achieved by the lateral pterygoid muscle.

questions.stemHtml: The pointed structure supplies all the following parts of the conducting system in the heart:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) SA node

 

The pointed structure in the image is the right coronary artery. The right coronary artery primarily supplies blood to the SA node (sinoatrial node) and part of the right atrium. It is also responsible for supplying the AV node in most individuals, but it does not supply the AV bundle (bundle of His) or the left bundle branch, which are mainly supplied by the left coronary artery and its branches.

 

The right coronary artery arises from the right aortic sinus and runs along the atrioventricular groove, giving off branches like the SA nodal branch.

 

The AV bundle and left bundle branch are primarily supplied by the left anterior descending artery, which is a branch of the left coronary artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. AV bundle: The AV bundle is supplied by the left anterior descending artery and not the right coronary artery.

 

Option C. Left bundle branch: The left bundle branch is supplied by the left anterior descending artery as well.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The right coronary artery supplies the SA node and parts of the AV node, but it does not supply the AV bundle or the left bundle branch.

questions.stemHtml: Injury to the artery that lies beneath the arrow will lead to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Extradural hemorrhage

 

The arrow in the image is pointing to the pterion, a region where several cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid) meet. Just beneath this area lies the middle meningeal artery, which is vulnerable to injury in cases of trauma to the lateral skull, such as a blow to the head.

 

If the middle meningeal artery is ruptured, it leads to an extradural (epidural) hemorrhage, characterized by the accumulation of blood between the dura mater and the skull. This is often associated with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurological deterioration if not treated promptly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subarachnoid haemorrhage: This occurs due to bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from a ruptured aneurysm or trauma to vessels in that space and is not associated with damage to the middle meningeal artery.

 

Option C. Subdural hemorrhage: Subdural hemorrhage results from tearing of bridging veins between the dura and arachnoid mater, typically in cases of shearing injury, not from injury to the middle meningeal artery.

 

Option D. Intraparenchymal haemorrhage: This refers to bleeding within the brain tissue itself, which is often caused by hypertension or trauma but does not involve the middle meningeal artery.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Injury to the middle meningeal artery located beneath the pterion can cause an extradural hemorrhage, a life-threatening condition that requires immediate medical attention.

questions.stem: Which artery can be palpated by gently pressing your fingers between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior tibial artery

 

The posterior tibial artery can be palpated by pressing between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon. This artery runs along the posterior aspect of the leg and provides blood to the foot and lower leg. Its pulsation is often checked to assess blood flow to the foot and is a key pulse point in clinical examinations for peripheral vascular disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior tibial artery: This artery runs on the anterior aspect of the leg and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery, but it is not located near the medial malleolus.

 

Option C. Dorsalis pedis artery: This artery is located on the dorsum of the foot and can be palpated on the top of the foot, not between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon.

 

Option D. Popliteal artery: The popliteal artery is located behind the knee and cannot be palpated in the area between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The posterior tibial artery is palpated between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon and is an important pulse point for assessing blood flow to the foot.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with complaints of recurrent episodes of food getting stuck in his throat, particularly after swallowing large pieces of meat. He describes a sensation of food bolus obstruction in the lower neck area. Barium swallow reveals an outpouching in the posterior wall of the hypopharynx. This clinical condition is located between which two muscles?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus

 

The condition described is most consistent with a Zenker's diverticulum, which is an outpouching of the posterior pharyngeal wall. This occurs at a weak point between the Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus muscles, specifically in a region known as Killian's dehiscence. A Zenker's diverticulum often leads to symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and the sensation of food being stuck in the throat. It is commonly identified through barium swallow studies.

 

The Cricopharyngeus muscle is part of the upper esophageal sphincter and is involved in opening and closing the esophagus during swallowing. Weakness or dysfunction at the junction between this muscle and the Thyropharyngeus muscle can lead to the formation of the diverticulum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Palatopharyngeus and Cricopharyngeus: These muscles are not involved in the location where Zenker's diverticulum occurs.

 

Option B. Thyropharyngeus and Palatopharyngeus: While both are pharyngeal muscles, they are not involved in the formation of the diverticulum.

 

Option D. Palatopharyngeus and Salpingopharyngeus: These muscles are not related to the anatomical site of Zenker's diverticulum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A Zenker's diverticulum forms between the Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus muscles, leading to a pouch in the posterior hypopharynx.

questions.stem: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pivot joint

 

Supination and pronation of the forearm occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, both of which are examples of pivot joints. These joints allow the radius to rotate around the ulna, facilitating the movements of supination (turning the palm upward) and pronation (turning the palm downward). A pivot joint permits rotation around a single axis, making it ideal for such rotational movements.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Saddle joint: Saddle joints allow for movement in two planes, such as in the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, but they are not involved in rotation like supination and pronation.

 

Option C. Ellipsoid joint: Also known as a condyloid joint, this type of joint allows movement in two planes (flexion-extension and abduction-adduction), but not rotation.

 

Option D. Ball and socket joint: These joints, such as the shoulder and hip joints, allow for movement in multiple planes, including rotation, but they are not involved in forearm supination and pronation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pivot joints, such as the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, are responsible for the rotational movements of supination and pronation in the forearm.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure is advised to occlude in ligation of the splenic artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) D

 

The splenic artery runs alongside the pancreas and supplies blood to the spleen. When ligating the splenic artery, the goal is to control bleeding, especially in cases like splenectomy or trauma to the spleen. The most appropriate point of ligation is at the splenic artery near the hilum of the spleen, which is represented by the structure labeled D in the image. Ligation here ensures control of blood flow to the spleen while preserving the integrity of other nearby structures such as the stomach and pancreas.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. B: This option does not represent the appropriate location for splenic artery ligation.

 

Option B. A: This structure is not involved in the process of controlling blood flow to the spleen.

 

Option D. C: This is not the ideal point for controlling blood supply to the spleen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ligation of the splenic artery should occur at the hilum of the spleen to effectively manage blood flow and prevent excessive bleeding.
